title: $100,000 OPT fee clears White House review: what comes next for foreign graduates
excerpt: DHS's proposal to attach a six-figure fee to the work program used by more than 300,000 international students a year has cleared White House regulatory review. Indian students — the largest OPT users — have the most at stake.
body:
• A Department of Homeland Security proposal to impose a $100,000 fee on Optional Practical Training (OPT) has cleared review at the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs — the final step before formal publication as a rule.
  • About 300,000 F-1 students used OPT employment authorization last year; the program lets graduates work up to 12 months — 36 months for STEM fields — and is the main bridge from a U.S. degree to H-1B sponsorship.
  • It remains unclear who would pay the fee — students, universities or employers — and DHS says "no policy should be considered final until it is formally announced."
  • Next steps: formal publication in the Federal Register, a public comment period and near-certain legal challenges, mirroring the court fight that blocked a similar $100,000 H-1B fee.

A proposal to charge international graduates $100,000 to work in the United States after finishing their degrees has cleared a mandatory White House review, bringing the most drastic change ever proposed to the Optional Practical Training program a step closer to reality.

The Department of Homeland Security submitted the proposal (RIN: 1653-AB01) to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs in late August, according to Bloomberg Law's reporting, and government records now show it has cleared that review. The OIRA notice did not include details on the proposal, but DHS is reportedly considering a $100,000 fee attached to OPT — the program that lets F-1 visa holders work in roles related to their studies for up to 12 months after graduation, with a 24-month extension for science, technology, engineering and mathematics fields. About 300,000 students on F-1 visas had employment authorization through OPT last year, per Bloomberg Law; the Hindu BusinessLine reported that roughly 419,000 foreigners were working on OPT in 2024.

A reversal of a campaign promise

The proposal would mark a stark departure from President Donald Trump's own 2024 campaign position. On an episode of the All-In podcast in 2024, he said: "What I want to do and what I will do is you graduate from a college, I think you should get automatically as part of your diploma a green card to be able to stay in this country. And that includes junior colleges too, anybody graduates from a college. You go there for two years or four years."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=zBuUIumENhY

"What I want to do and what I will do is you graduate from a college, I think you should get automatically as part of your diploma a green card to be able to stay in this country."

— President Donald Trump, on the All-In podcast, 2024

A $100,000 levy on the work authorization that follows graduation would, in practice, do the opposite — crippling many graduates' ability to stay.

The context: the H-1B fee fight and the end of Duration of Status

The OPT fee is not arriving in isolation. In September 2025, the administration issued a proclamation requiring employers to pay a $100,000 fee to sponsor H-1B workers; a federal court blocked it, and an appeal was rejected on July 24, 2026. Separately, a 2025 proposal to end "Duration of Status" — the decades-old rule that let international students stay as long as their studies required — is expected to become a rule in September 2026, limiting students to four years unless an extension is approved by immigration officials.

Analysts see the OPT fee as another route to the same goal. Immigration monitors note that a six-figure OPT fee could achieve what the blocked H-1B fee was designed to do: pricing out a large share of international graduates from the U.S. labor market.

What it means for Indian students

Indians are the largest national group among international students in the United States and among OPT users, so no community would feel a six-figure OPT fee more sharply. The open question is who pays: if students bear it, few could afford to stay; if employers pay, many may simply stop hiring OPT graduates; if universities are tapped, costs could flow into tuition. Either way, the economics of a U.S. degree — already weighed against rising tuition — change dramatically, and competing destinations such as Canada, the U.K. and Australia stand to benefit.

What happens next

Clearing OIRA review means the proposal moves toward formal publication in the Federal Register, where a public comment period will follow before any final rule. Lawsuits are widely expected — the H-1B fee's defeat in court is the template. "No policies should be considered final until formally announced," a DHS spokeswoman said, adding that the department is "always having conversations about how to use all tools in our arsenal to protect the integrity of our legal immigration system." Until the rule's text is published, universities and students are in wait-and-see mode.
image_caption: An illustration shows the White House, a graduation cap and a $100,000 price tag. The Department of Homeland Security is proposing a six-figure fee for the Optional Practical Training program used by international graduates.
nri_angle: Indians form the largest group of OPT users, so a six-figure fee would reshape the economics of a U.S. degree for Indian families more than any other community.
